vignette:
He is a 71-year-old North American man who has spent most of his adult life working as an insurance agent, a job that suited him because it gave him a clear script, a desk between himself and other people, and enough structure to keep his thoughts organized. He presents as careful and composed, but as he talks over several sessions, his life begins to feel arranged around an old fear that never fully left him.

He grows up in a home where a caregiver’s mood can change without warning. As a child, he learns to listen for footsteps in the hall and the tone of a voice before he can trust the words being spoken. Discipline is not correction but punishment, and punishment often arrives in the form of hands, belts, or objects grabbed in anger. He remembers the anticipation most vividly: the tightening in his stomach, the feeling that he must become very small and very still, hoping to avoid notice. He does not think of himself as a child with needs so much as a child trying not to trigger the next blow.

Even now, he describes that period in fragments rather than a continuous story, as if the memories were stored in separate rooms. There are details he can summon instantly—the smell of a hallway, the sound of a radio playing in the next room, the exact way his body would brace when he heard a door slam—but he has long struggled to put the whole thing into words. He says that as a boy he became good at reading people because it felt necessary for survival. That same vigilance follows him into adulthood. He is often aware of who is standing too close, who sounds irritated, who might be about to lose control. He tells himself he is simply observant, but his body reacts before his mind can reassure him.

As a young man, leaving home brings relief, though not freedom. He builds a life that looks orderly from the outside. He dresses neatly, arrives early, and keeps his paperwork in perfect stacks. Insurance work becomes a natural fit because it rewards caution, thoroughness, and the ability to anticipate what could go wrong. He is known as dependable, even unflappable. Colleagues appreciate that he does not make trouble and clients trust his calm demeanor. He rarely discusses his personal life. He has never married, and his relationships stay limited, partly because closeness feels risky and partly because he has learned to function best when no one expects too much from him.

Underneath that steadiness, however, he lives with an ongoing tension that he has normalized over the decades. He startles easily at sudden movements or raised voices. He avoids confrontation and will apologize quickly, even when he has done nothing wrong. In meetings, if someone speaks sharply, he feels heat rush through his chest and shoulders, and his mind goes blank for a moment before he can gather himself. At home, he keeps his environment quiet and controlled. He checks locks twice, sometimes three times, and he dislikes unexpected visitors. He says he is simply set in his ways, though he also admits that surprises make his heart race and leave him irritated for reasons he cannot always explain.

Nighttime is harder. He sleeps lightly and wakes often, especially if a dream has carried him back into a room where he cannot move fast enough to protect himself. He does not always remember the dream, only the residue of it: a pounding heartbeat, clenched jaw, and a lingering sense that something bad is about to happen. Some mornings he sits at the kitchen table for a long time before starting the day, feeling older than his age and strangely far from his own body. On certain anniversaries or during family gatherings, he notices an old sadness rising up alongside a sharp anger that has nowhere to go. He has spent years believing that what happened in childhood was simply part of life, yet he also recognizes how often his present is governed by the past.

Recently, he has become more aware of the cost of carrying so much for so long. He feels lonely at times, though he finds it difficult to let others in. He wants connection, but trust comes slowly, and his first instinct is still to protect himself by holding back. When he speaks about his childhood now, there is grief in his voice, and also disbelief that a child could be treated that way and still be expected to grow into a whole man. He sits in the office with his hands folded carefully, a habit that makes him look composed even when his eyes become wet. His life has been built on competence and self-control, yet beneath that surface he remains a man who learned early that danger could come from the very person meant to keep him safe.
